# Auriora

> Auriora is an open research initiative exploring how intelligence emerges across very different systems through observation, measurement and open experimentation. It is building open instruments to study sensing, adaptation and communication, beginning with plants and the networks they live in. It does not start from a definition of intelligence; it starts from what can be measured.

Auriora is not a theory to defend, but a question to explore: What is intelligence, and how does it emerge in different systems? The work is open, and it is supported by openly developed instruments, standards, experiments and shared research.

- Site: https://auriora.org/
- GitHub: https://github.com/auriora-org
- Single-page website (English). All sections below are anchors on the home page.
- Contact: contact@auriora.org

## Vision

Understanding intelligence beyond familiar boundaries. Intelligence usually means brains. Yet a root or a fungal network responds to its surroundings with no nervous system at all, and an ant colony coordinates thousands of individuals with no central control. These are different kinds of organization, and sensing and responding are not the same as intelligence. But they can be measured, and that makes them a place to start. Auriora takes this seriously: it is building open instruments to record how plants signal and respond, and develops them in public. Whether the word intelligence reaches that far is a result Auriora is after, not an assumption it starts from.

- [Vision](https://auriora.org/#vision)

## The question

What is intelligence, and how does it emerge in different systems? Most of us think we know intelligence when we see it, yet it is hard to say what actually makes a system intelligent. A dog that has been to the vet once refuses the car the next time; a bean seedling turns toward the window within a day, and its root changes course when it meets a stone; an ant colony has no one in charge, yet it reroutes when the path to food is blocked. Each takes in something from its surroundings and changes what it does because of it. Whether that deserves the same word in every case is exactly what is not known. What, if anything, do these systems have in common, and is it the same thing we mean when we say intelligence?

- [The question](https://auriora.org/#question)

## An open question

Why do we still struggle to explain intelligence? Partly because most of what we know comes from humans and other animals, and concepts built around nervous systems travel badly to a root tip or a mycelium. Partly because the measurements are hard to compare: plant signaling has been studied experimentally for more than a century, but a recording depends on the electrode, the plant, the room and the stimulus, and unless all of that is documented, one study cannot easily be checked against the next. There is still no agreed answer to what intelligence is, whether it comes down to one mechanism, or why it shows up where it does. Auriora does not expect that answer to come from arguing about definitions, but from observations that can be compared and repeated, made in the open.

- [Open question](https://auriora.org/#open-question)

## Principles

How do we explore the unknown? Measure before interpreting: the recording comes first, and the explanation is allowed to change when the next recording disagrees with it. Everything Auriora makes is meant to stay open: the instrument designs, the methods, the raw data and the reasoning that connects them; if a result cannot be reproduced from what is published, that is treated as a bug. Careful engineering is not a separate concern from careful science: a signal is only as trustworthy as the tool that recorded it.

- [Principles](https://auriora.org/#principles)

## Focus

Starting where the signals are measurable. If intelligence is more widespread than our categories assume, the place to find out is where the signals can actually be recorded. Auriora begins with plants, whose signals can be recorded with instruments it can build and share. The fungi and networks around them come later. It does not begin by assuming that plants are intelligent and then set out to prove it; it begins with what these systems measurably do and lets the evidence decide what the word means here. The signal channels in focus:

- Electrical signaling: action, variation and systemic potentials, the fast, long-distance signals that travel through living tissue.
- Chemical signaling: volatile and chemical cues between plants and their surroundings. A later direction, not one Auriora measures yet.
- Light and photobiology: how living systems read the spectrum, direction and timing of light, and reshape themselves in response.
- Sound and vibration: mechanical and acoustic signals as stimuli, and potentially as information the organism acts on.

- [Focus](https://auriora.org/#focus)

## Direction

Beyond familiar definitions. Plants are the starting point, not the boundary. Once the methods are reliable in plants, the interesting question is how other living systems sense, respond and adapt, from fungal networks and colonies to lineages that parted ways with plants more than a billion years ago. A familiar-looking signal is only a clue, and what it does for the organism matters more. The similarities will be telling, and so will the differences. Auriora is not a theory of intelligence. It is a place to work on the question in public, with instruments and data anyone can check. Its direction: new perspectives (human cognition is one case among many, not the yardstick), open research (designs, data and arguments are published, so being wrong is easy to show), beyond the human (plants first, because their signals can be recorded with instruments that can be built today, fungi and other systems after), and shared discovery (nobody owns the question; work from any field is welcome, and credited).

- [Direction](https://auriora.org/#direction)

## What we are building

Instruments for open exploration. A question this open needs instruments and repeatable results. Auriora is developing an open, modular platform for measuring and stimulating living systems in step, so that measurement, stimulation and recording form one documented experiment. The first modules in development record plant electrical signals and stimulate with light and sound, built to run together. They are a starting point, not the scope. The platform is meant to grow as new research questions call for new instruments. Everything is built in the open under one engineering standard for hardware, firmware, software and documentation. Reproducibility is concrete: open designs, versioned interfaces, documented calibration, and timing recorded with the data, so an experiment can be repeated, not merely described. The standards are already public, and the instrument repositories follow as each module is ready for release. If you study plant or network behavior, these instruments are being built for you to use, question and improve. To take part, write to contact@auriora.org.

- [Building](https://auriora.org/#building)
- [GitHub organization](https://github.com/auriora-org)
